steps.prompt: What is the difference between don’t have to and can’t?
options: Don’t have to = it isn’t necessary. Can’t = it isn’t allowed.
They both mean the same thing: that it is completely forbidden.
They both mean the same thing: that it is absolutely necessary.
steps.answer: Don’t have to = it isn’t necessary. Can’t = it isn’t allowed.
steps.why: This is the biggest trap in the topic: don’t have to is freedom, can’t and mustn’t are prohibition.

steps.title: must, have to, don’t have to, can
steps.html:
MeaningFormExample
it is necessarymust / have toYou have to arrive on time.
I feel it is importantmustYou must ask when you don’t understand.
it is not necessarydon’t have toYou don’t have to finish everything.
it is not allowedcan’t / mustn’tYou can’t say ‘I’m bad at this’.
it is allowedcanYou can say ‘I can’t do it yet’.
in the pasthad to / couldn’tWe had to knock. We couldn’t use phones.

Must and can take the base form and never change: he must, she can — no -s, no to.

Have to behaves like a normal verb: he has to, they don’t have to, did you have to?

Must usually comes from the speaker; have to usually comes from a rule outside. In everyday English have to is far more common.

Must has no past. Use had to: We had to knock, never we musted.

You met can for ability in the last lesson. Here it means permission — same word, different job.

steps.title: The classroom that worked
steps.html:
Four rules, and what happened in two years.

Reading

For eleven years Room 9 was the class nobody wanted. Then a teacher called Bekzat took it, and in two years it had the best grades in the school. People came to watch. What they found was not a method. It was four rules.

You have to arrive on time. Not “you should”. The door closed at 8.30 and after that you had to knock and say why. “It sounds strict,” Bekzat says. “It isn’t about the clock. It is the first promise of the day, and it is easy to keep.”

You must ask when you don’t understand. Every student had to ask at least one question a week. At first they invented questions. By November they were asking real ones.

You don’t have to finish everything. This one surprised the visitors. Homework had a time limit, not a page limit: forty minutes, and then you stop. “A student who works until midnight is not a better student,” he says. “They are a tired one.”

You can’t say ‘I’m bad at this’. You can say “I can’t do it yet”. The word yet was on the wall in letters thirty centimetres high.

Bekzat has no degree in education; his qualification is in maths. “I don’t have to be a psychologist,” he says. “I have to be the same person on Monday that I was on Friday.”

steps.sub: Six rules. Use a different form in each one.
steps.html:
1. Plan: something necessary → something you feel is important → something optional → something forbidden → something allowed → one rule from the past.
  • You have to …
  • You must …
  • You don’t have to …
  • You can’t …
  • You can …
  • When I was at school we had to …

steps.modelHtml:
• I wrote six rules.
  • One uses have to and one uses must.
  • One uses don’t have to for something optional.
  • One uses can’t or mustn’t for something forbidden.
  • One is in the past with had to or couldn’t.

steps.title: Say the rules out loud, then record them.
steps.sub: Tap a line to hear a model first.
items: You have to arrive before half past eight.
You must ask when you don’t understand something.
You don’t have to finish the whole page.
You can’t use your phone during the lesson.
When I was at school we had to wear a uniform.
